hello.note: Works any time of day, with anyone

good-morning.note: Most people just say 안녕하세요 (ahn-nyoung-ha-se-yo) all day

good-night.note: Polite, literally "sleep in peace". To friends, 잘 자 (jal ja)

goodbye.note: Said when you leave and the other person stays. When they are the one leaving, say 안녕히 가세요 (ahn-nyoung-hee ga-se-yo)

please.note: Means "please give me" and goes after what you want: 물 주세요 (mool ju-se-yo), water please

thank-you.note: 고마워요 (go-ma-wo-yo) is a little less formal

yes.note: 예 (ye) is a more formal yes

excuse-me.note: Says sorry. To get attention, such as a waiter's, call 저기요 (juh-gi-yo)

my-name.note: The audio uses 피터 (pi-tuh), Peter, as the example name

one.note: The numbers for prices, money and phone numbers. Counting things uses a native set: 하나 (ha-na), 둘 (dool), 셋 (set)

four.note: Sounds like the word for death, so lifts often show F instead of 4

thousand.note: Prices are in won. 10,000 is 만 (man)

hundred-thousand.note: Literally ten 만 (man): Korean counts big numbers in ten thousands

would-like.note: Put what you want first. The audio uses 커피 (kuh-pi), coffee, as the example

i-want.note: Literally "I need...": Korean rarely says "I want" about things. The audio uses 이거 (i-guh), this, as the example

do-you-have.note: Put the item first. The audio uses 물 (mool), water, as the example

discount.note: Haggling is normal at traditional markets, not in shops

card.note: Literally "is card OK?" Cards are taken almost everywhere

bill.note: In many restaurants you pay at the counter on the way out

bus-station.note: For long-distance buses. A bus stop is 버스 정류장 (buh-seu jung-nyu-jang)

train-station.note: 역 (yuk) alone is any station, including the underground

which-train.note: The audio uses 부산 (boo-san), Busan, as the example

two-tickets.note: 장 (jang) counts tickets and other flat things. The audio uses Busan as the example

trip-length.note: The audio uses Busan as the example

allergic.note: Put the food first: 해산물 (hae-san-mul) seafood, 견과류 (gyun-gwa-ryu) nuts, 땅콩 (ttang-kong) peanuts, 계란 (gye-ran) eggs. The audio uses seafood as the example

what-called.note: Literally "what is this?" Point at the dish or item

table-for-two.note: Literally "two people", what you say at the door. For more: 세 명 (se myung), 3, or 네 명 (ne myung), 4

recommend.note: Literally "what is good here?", the usual way to ask

water.note: Water is usually free in restaurants, often self-service

cheers.note: When drinking with older people, turn your head slightly away as you drink

help.note: Shout it. The police are on 112
